sentences.text: One of the most common types of advice we give at Y Combinator is to do things that don't scale.
sentences.subject: Do Things that Don't Scale

sentences.text: A lot of would-be founders believe that startups either take off or don't.
sentences.subject: Do Things that Don't Scale

sentences.text: Actually startups take off because the founders make them take off.
sentences.subject: Do Things that Don't Scale

sentences.text: There may be a handful that just grew by themselves, but usually it takes some sort of push to get them going.
sentences.subject: Do Things that Don't Scale

sentences.text: Once the engine was going, it would keep going, but there was a separate and laborious process to get it going.
sentences.subject: Do Things that Don't Scale

sentences.text: The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: Nearly all startups have to.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: You can't wait for users to come to you.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: You have to go out and get them.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: But in fact they're famous within YC for aggressive early user acquisition.
sentences.subject: Stripe

sentences.text: At YC we use the term "Collison installation" for the technique they invented.
sentences.subject: Stripe

sentences.text: When anyone agreed to try Stripe they'd say "Right then, give me your laptop" and set them up on the spot.
sentences.subject: Stripe

sentences.text: There are two reasons founders resist going out and recruiting users individually.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: One is a combination of shyness and laziness.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: But for a startup to succeed, at least one founder (usually the CEO) will have to spend a lot of time on sales and marketing.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: The other reason founders ignore this path is that the absolute numbers seem so small at first.
sentences.subject: compound growth

sentences.text: The mistake they make is to underestimate the power of compound growth.
sentences.subject: compound growth

sentences.text: We encourage every startup to measure their progress by weekly growth rate.
sentences.subject: compound growth

sentences.text: And while 110 may not seem much better than 100, if you keep growing at 10% a week you'll be surprised how big the numbers get.
sentences.subject: compound growth

sentences.text: After a year you'll have 14,000 users, and after 2 years you'll have 2 million.
sentences.subject: compound growth

sentences.text: But if the market exists you can usually start by recruiting users manually and then gradually switch to less manual methods.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: Marketplaces are so hard to get rolling that you should expect to take heroic measures at first.
sentences.subject: Airbnb

sentences.text: In Airbnb's case, these consisted of going door to door in New York, recruiting new users and helping existing ones improve their listings.
sentences.subject: Airbnb

sentences.text: Airbnb now seems like an unstoppable juggernaut, but early on it was so fragile that about 30 days of going out and engaging in person with users made the difference between success and failure.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: That initial fragility was not a unique feature of Airbnb.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: Almost all startups are fragile initially.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: And that's one of the biggest things inexperienced founders and investors (and reporters and know-it-alls on forums) get wrong about them.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: They unconsciously judge larval startups by the standards of established ones.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: The big danger is that you'll dismiss your startup yourself.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: The question to ask about an early stage startup is not "is this company taking over the world?" but "how big could this company get if the founders did the right things?" And the right things often seem both laborious and inconsequential at the time.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: Microsoft can't have seemed very impressive when it was just a couple guys in Albuquerque writing Basic interpreters for a market of a few thousand hobbyists (as they were then called), but in retrospect that was the optimal path to dominating microcomputer software.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: But in retrospect that too was the optimal path to dominating a big market.
sentences.subject: Fragile

sentences.text: If you build something to solve your own problems, then you only have to find your peers, which is usually straightforward.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: Otherwise you'll have to make a more deliberate effort to locate the most promising vein of users.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: The usual way to do that is to get some initial set of users by doing a comparatively untargeted launch, and then to observe which kind seem most enthusiastic, and seek out more like them.
sentences.subject: Recruit

sentences.text: You should take extraordinary measures not just to acquire users, but also to make them happy.
sentences.subject: Delight

sentences.text: For as long as they could (which turned out to be surprisingly long), Wufoo sent each new user a hand-written thank you note.
sentences.subject: Delight

sentences.text: Your first users should feel that signing up with you was one of the best choices they ever made.
sentences.subject: Delight

sentences.text: And you in turn should be racking your brains to think of new ways to delight them.
sentences.subject: Delight

sentences.text: One is that a lot of startup founders are trained as engineers, and customer service is not part of the training of engineers.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: You're supposed to build things that are robust and elegant, not be slavishly attentive to individual users like some kind of salesperson.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: Another reason founders don't focus enough on individual customers is that they worry it won't scale.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: But when founders of larval startups worry about this, I point out that in their current state they have nothing to lose.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: And incidentally, when it does, you'll find that delighting customers scales better than you expected.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: I have never once seen a startup lured down a blind alley by trying too hard to make their initial users happy.
sentences.subject: Delight

sentences.text: But perhaps the biggest thing preventing founders from realizing how attentive they could be to their users is that they've never experienced such attention themselves.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: Their standards for customer service have been set by the companies they've been customers of, which are mostly big ones.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: That's one advantage of being small: you can provide a level of service no big company can.
sentences.subject: customer service

sentences.text: Once you realize that existing conventions are not the upper bound on user experience, it's interesting in a very pleasant way to think about how far you could go to delight your users.
sentences.subject: Delight

sentences.text: I was trying to think of a phrase to convey how extreme your attention to users should be, and I realized Steve Jobs had already done it: insanely great.
sentences.subject: insanely great

sentences.text: Steve wasn't just using "insanely" as a synonym for "very." He meant it more literally — that one should focus on quality of execution to a degree that in everyday life would be considered pathological.
sentences.subject: insanely great

sentences.text: What novice founders don't get is what insanely great translates to in a larval startup.
sentences.subject: insanely great

sentences.text: What founders have a hard time grasping (and Steve himself might have had a hard time grasping) is what insanely great morphs into as you roll the time slider back to the first couple months of a startup's life.
sentences.subject: insanely great

sentences.text: It's not the product that should be insanely great, but the experience of being your user.
sentences.subject: insanely great

sentences.text: The product is just one component of that.
sentences.subject: insanely great

sentences.text: But you can and should give users an insanely great experience with an early, incomplete, buggy product, if you make up the difference with attentiveness.
sentences.subject: insanely great

sentences.text: Over-engaging with early users is not just a permissible technique for getting growth rolling.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: For most successful startups it's a necessary part of the feedback loop that makes the product good.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: Making a better mousetrap is not an atomic operation.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: Even if you start the way most successful startups have, by building something you yourself need, the first thing you build is never quite right.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: And except in domains with big penalties for making mistakes, it's often better not to aim for perfection initially.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: In software, especially, it usually works best to get something in front of users as soon as it has a quantum of utility, and then see what they do with it.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: Perfectionism is often an excuse for procrastination, and in any case your initial model of users is always inaccurate, even if you're one of them.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: The feedback you get from engaging directly with your earliest users will be the best you ever get.
sentences.subject: feedback loop

sentences.text: Sometimes the right unscalable trick is to focus on a deliberately narrow market.
sentences.subject: Fire

sentences.text: It's like keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot before adding more logs.
sentences.subject: Fire

sentences.text: In that form it only had a potential market of a few thousand people, but because they felt it was really for them, a critical mass of them signed up.
sentences.subject: Fire

sentences.text: Any startup that could be described as a marketplace usually has to start in a subset of the market, but this can work for other startups as well.
sentences.subject: Fire

sentences.text: It's always worth asking if there's a subset of the market in which you can get a critical mass of users quickly.
sentences.subject: Fire

sentences.text: Most startups that use the contained fire strategy do it unconsciously.
sentences.subject: Fire

sentences.text: Among companies, the best early adopters are usually other startups.
sentences.subject: early adopters

sentences.text: They're more open to new things both by nature and because, having just been started, they haven't made all their choices yet.
sentences.subject: early adopters

sentences.text: For hardware startups there's a variant of doing things that don't scale that we call "pulling a Meraki." Although we didn't fund Meraki, the founders were Robert Morris's grad students, so we know their history.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: They got started by doing something that really doesn't scale: assembling their routers themselves.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: Hardware startups face an obstacle that software startups don't.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: The minimum order for a factory production run is usually several hundred thousand dollars.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: Which can put you in a catch-22: without a product you can't generate the growth you need to raise the money to manufacture your product.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: But even so I'd advise startups to pull a Meraki initially if they can.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: If they hadn't gone through that phase, they probably wouldn't have sold $10 million worth of watches when they did go on Kickstarter.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: Like paying excessive attention to early customers, fabricating things yourself turns out to be valuable for hardware startups.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: You can tweak the design faster when you're the factory, and you learn things you'd never have known otherwise.
sentences.subject: Meraki

sentences.text: Sometimes we advise founders of B2B startups to take over-engagement to an extreme, and to pick a single user and act as if they were consultants building something just for that one user.
sentences.subject: Consult

sentences.text: The initial user serves as the form for your mold; keep tweaking till you fit their needs perfectly, and you'll usually find you've made something other users want too.
sentences.subject: Consult

sentences.text: As long as you can find just one user who really needs something and can act on that need, you've got a toehold in making something people want, and that's as much as any startup needs initially.
sentences.subject: Consult

sentences.text: Consulting is the canonical example of work that doesn't scale.
sentences.subject: Consult

sentences.text: But (like other ways of bestowing one's favors liberally) it's safe to do it so long as you're not being paid to.
sentences.subject: Consult

sentences.text: So long as you're a product company that's merely being extra attentive to a customer, they're very grateful even if you don't solve all their problems.
sentences.subject: Consult

sentences.text: But when they start paying you specifically for that attentiveness — when they start paying you by the hour — they expect you to do everything.
sentences.subject: Consult

sentences.text: Another consulting-like technique for recruiting initially lukewarm users is to use your software yourselves on their behalf.
sentences.subject: Viaweb

sentences.text: But in retrospect it was exactly the right thing to do, because it taught us how it would feel to merchants to use our software.
sentences.subject: Viaweb

sentences.text: Sometimes the feedback loop was near instantaneous: in the middle of building some merchant's site I'd find I needed a feature we didn't have, so I'd spend a couple hours implementing it and then resume building the site.
sentences.subject: Viaweb

sentences.text: There's a more extreme variant where you don't just use your software, but are your software.
sentences.subject: Manual

sentences.text: When you only have a small number of users, you can sometimes get away with doing by hand things that you plan to automate later.
sentences.subject: Manual

sentences.text: This lets you launch faster, and when you do finally automate yourself out of the loop, you'll know exactly what to build because you'll have muscle memory from doing it yourself.
sentences.subject: Manual

sentences.text: For example, the way Stripe delivered "instant" merchant accounts to its first users was that the founders manually signed them up for traditional merchant accounts behind the scenes.
sentences.subject: Manual

sentences.text: If you can find someone with a problem that needs solving and you can solve it manually, go ahead and do that for as long as you can, and then gradually automate the bottlenecks.
sentences.subject: Manual

sentences.text: It would be a little frightening to be solving users' problems in a way that wasn't yet automatic, but less frightening than the far more common case of having something automatic that doesn't yet solve anyone's problems.
sentences.subject: Manual

sentences.text: I should mention one sort of initial tactic that usually doesn't work: the Big Launch.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: I occasionally meet founders who seem to believe startups are projectiles rather than powered aircraft, and that they'll make it big if and only if they're launched with sufficient initial velocity.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: It's easy to see how little launches matter.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: All you need from a launch is some initial core of users.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: How well you're doing a few months later will depend more on how happy you made those users than how many there were of them.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: They think what they're building is so great that everyone who hears about it will immediately sign up.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: But even if what you're building really is great, getting users will always be a gradual process — partly because great things are usually also novel, but mainly because users have other things to think about.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: Partnerships too usually don't work.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: It's a common mistake among inexperienced founders to believe that a partnership with a big company will be their big break.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: It's not enough just to do something extraordinary initially.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: You have to make an extraordinary effort initially.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: Any strategy that omits the effort — whether it's expecting a big launch to get you users, or a big partner — is ipso facto suspect.
sentences.subject: Big

sentences.text: The need to do something unscalably laborious to get started is so nearly universal that it might be a good idea to stop thinking of startup ideas as scalars.
sentences.subject: Vector

sentences.text: Instead we should try thinking of them as pairs of what you're going to build, plus the unscalable thing(s) you're going to do initially to get the company going.
sentences.subject: Vector

sentences.text: But in most cases the second component will be what it usually is — recruit users manually and give them an overwhelmingly good experience — and the main benefit of treating startups as vectors will be to remind founders they need to work hard in two dimensions.
sentences.subject: Vector

sentences.text: In the best case, both components of the vector contribute to your company's DNA: the unscalable things you have to do to get started are not merely a necessary evil, but change the company permanently for the better.
sentences.subject: Vector

sentences.text: If you have to be aggressive about user acquisition when you're small, you'll probably still be aggressive when you're big.
sentences.subject: Vector

sentences.text: If you have to manufacture your own hardware, or use your software on users's behalf, you'll learn things you couldn't have learned otherwise.
sentences.subject: Vector

sentences.text: And most importantly, if you have to work hard to delight users when you only have a handful of them, you'll keep doing it when you have a lot.
sentences.subject: Vector
